body:
Eel Pie Island is easy to reach and difficult to visit. From Twickenham’s Church Street, a short lane runs to a footbridge over the Thames. The bridge makes the island look public, but it is not an everyday attraction. Beyond it are private homes, working boatyards and artists’ studios. Unless you are invited or attending an official Open Studios event, the respectful visit stops at the riverbank.

That restriction is not an inconvenience to work around. It is part of the island’s continued existence as a community rather than a themed reconstruction of its past. The useful question is not how to get onto Eel Pie Island at any time. It is when access is genuinely offered, what the island has been, and how much of its story can still be understood from Twickenham.

## Start with the view from the riverbank

The best everyday introduction is the Thames path and Embankment on the Twickenham side. From here the footbridge, boats, slipways, trees and irregular riverside buildings overlap in a way that explains the island better than one postcard façade. Tides alter the amount of exposed river edge and the position of moored boats, so the view never feels fixed.

Continue through Church Street, then towards York House Gardens and the riverside. My own Facebook posts have returned to this sequence several times because it makes a satisfying short walk even when the island is closed: independent shops and cafés, the Thames, the bridge, the gardens and a pub stop can fill an unhurried afternoon without pretending you have entered a private place.

For the historical layer, the Eel Pie Island Museum on Richmond Road is the practical counterpart to the view. It brings together the music venue, boatyards, local characters, inventions and artists in a small space run by people who have spent years collecting the evidence. Check current opening days before travelling; it is volunteer-led and can close around local events.

## The hotel turned the island into Eelpiland

The island had been a riverside resort long before rock music arrived, but the Eel Pie Hotel created the mythology that still attracts attention. The museum records the first official Eel Pie Jazz Club performance on 10 August 1956, when Ken Colyer’s band played in the hotel ballroom. The new footbridge opened in February 1957, replacing the old ferry and making access far easier.

Traditional jazz dominated first. Rhythm and blues and rock followed, and between 1956 and 1970 the ballroom hosted an extraordinary roll-call that included the Rolling Stones, Jeff Beck, Rod Stewart, Eric Clapton and many others before they became part of the standard history of British music. The building was run-down, membership rules helped negotiate licensing restrictions, and the crossing itself made a night there feel separate from ordinary London.

It is tempting to compress all of this into a claim that every famous band played on the island. The museum’s detailed year-by-year listings are better than legend. They show changing promoters, genres and periods of closure rather than one uninterrupted golden age. The hotel no longer exists, so the history is carried by archives, memories and the continuing reputation of the place rather than a preserved stage.

## The boatyards are older than the music story

Focusing only on the bands misses the island’s working backbone. The museum traces continuous boatyard use on part of Eel Pie Island from 1892. Electric and steam launches, early petrol engines, repairs and river services all formed part of a landscape made more viable when Richmond Lock and Weir began maintaining a navigable level of water upstream.

Boatyards still operate here. During Open Studios, visitors pass spaces that are workplaces rather than scenery, and the organisers explicitly ask them to remain on the marked routes. Boats under repair, slipways, sheds and improvised storage explain why the island has resisted becoming polished.

That combination of creative use and river industry has a distant east-London echo at [Trinity Buoy Wharf](/journal/trinity-buoy-wharf-lighthouse/), where studios and working infrastructure also occupy the same ground. The two places are not interchangeable: Eel Pie is smaller, residential and normally private. The comparison is useful because both depend on activity, not just preserved appearance.

## Artists gave the island another life

A community of artists became established from the late 1980s, occupying studios across a landscape of gardens, workshops and boatyards. Today the official artists’ group includes painters, printmakers, illustrators, ceramicists, sculptors and makers working in very different visual languages. The island was also home to Trevor Baylis, inventor of the wind-up radio, whose workshop linked creativity with practical engineering.

Open Studios usually take place twice a year, commonly in early summer and early December. Recent events have been free but ticketed, with timed entry to control numbers. Dates and arrangements change, so the artists’ own website is the only sensible place to plan a visit. Do not rely on an old blog post or turn up because the bridge happens to be open.

When access is offered, the small details matter as much as the studios: a hand-painted book-swap box, improvised gates, eccentric notices, gardens assembled from found objects and buildings that appear to have evolved by addition rather than design. They are not props. They belong to a lived-in place, and visitors should photograph people or individual artworks only with permission.

The studio visits are the point, not a race to see every corner. Talk to makers, buy directly if something matters to you and accept that private houses and working areas remain off-limits even during the event.

## Access is limited for practical reasons too

The footbridge is steep, some studios have steps and the island’s working surfaces are uneven. The Open Studios organisers warn that wheelchair access is not available in every studio. Anyone with specific access needs should check the current event information before booking rather than infer conditions from the short distance on a map.

Families need the same realism. The island can be welcoming during public events, but it remains a working boatyard with water, machinery, narrow routes and private residences. Stay on the designated walkways and do not treat closed gates as a challenge.

Outside Open Studios, build the visit around Twickenham itself. The museum, Church Street, York House Gardens, Orleans House Gallery and a Thames walk provide a fuller day than standing at the bridge and resenting the boundary. If you want another west-London place where a house, garden and surrounding streets tell one connected story, our [Chiswick walk](/journal/chiswick-hogarth-house-gardens-mosaic-house/) offers a useful companion.

## The boundary protects the character people come to see

Eel Pie Island’s appeal rests on a contradiction. Its music history and eccentric image make people curious, while its privacy and continuing work prevent it from becoming a conventional visitor attraction. Removing that boundary would damage the qualities that created the curiosity.

Go to the riverbank at any time. Visit the museum to understand what you are looking at. Cross the bridge only when the island’s community officially invites the public in. That is not a lesser experience; it is the honest way to encounter a place that still belongs to the people who live and work there.
